title: Why GLP-1 Drugs Don't Work for Everyone
hook: Scientists found genetic variants — carried by roughly 1 in 10 people — that seem to cause a kind of 'GLP-1 resistance,' making drugs like Ozempic less effective at controlling blood sugar.
key_points: Researchers identified genetic variants linked to a poorer response to GLP-1 drugs for Type 2 diabetes.
About 10% of people carry these variants — a possible explanation for 'GLP-1 resistance.'
In several clinical trials, carriers were less likely to reach healthy blood sugar targets on GLP-1 medications.
Hints at a future where genetics helps predict who benefits most from a given drug.
content_html: GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide have become a mainstay for Type 2 diabetes and weight loss, but they don't help everyone equally. Scientists now report genetic variants that may explain why: carried by about 10% of people, they appear to cause a form of "GLP-1 resistance" that blunts the drug's effect. Across several clinical trials, people with these variants were significantly less likely to reach healthy blood sugar targets while taking the medications.
extra_html:
As ScienceDaily explains, the finding reframes a frustrating clinical reality — patients who do everything right yet see little benefit — as something rooted partly in their biology rather than effort or dosing alone. It's a reminder that "the drug didn't work" can sometimes mean "the drug doesn't fit this person."

The broader promise here is pharmacogenomics: using someone's genetics to predict which treatment will actually help before they spend months trying it. That future isn't here yet — these are research findings, not a test your doctor orders today — but identifying who responds, and who doesn't, is exactly the kind of knowledge that makes treatment less of a guessing game.

related.title: Preventing Type 2 Diabetes
related.hook: Type 2 diabetes often arrives slowly, with a warning stage called prediabetes — and at that stage, modest lifestyle changes can stop or delay it.

related.title: GLP-1 Drugs Linked to Lower Addiction Risk
related.hook: A study of ~600,000 U.S. veterans links GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide to lower rates of addiction and overdose — an association, not proof that the drugs cause the effect.

flashcards.prompt: Why might a GLP-1 drug fail to control blood sugar in some people?
flashcards.back_html: Some people carry genetic variants that appear to cause "GLP-1 resistance" — their bodies respond less to the medication. Roughly 1 in 10 people carry them, and in trials these carriers were less likely to hit healthy blood sugar targets.

flashcards.prompt: About what share of people carry the variants tied to GLP-1 resistance?
flashcards.explanation_html: Researchers estimate about 10% of the population carries these variants — common enough to help explain why the drugs work far better for some people than others.
